blocks.text: A healthy 28-year-old woman has had three miscarriages in two years. Her blood karyotype shows 45 chromosomes, not 46, yet she has no features of any syndrome and no genetic material appears to be missing. How can a person with a missing chromosome be perfectly healthy, and why does her family have a problem?

blocks.markdown: **Structural chromosome abnormalities** involve a change in the *structure* of a chromosome rather than its number. They arise from breakage of the DNA followed by incorrect rejoining, and may occur de novo or be inherited from a parent. The key clinical question is whether the rearrangement is **balanced** (no net gain or loss of genetic material) or **unbalanced** (net gain or loss).

blocks.title: Balanced and unbalanced rearrangements
blocks.text: A balanced rearrangement involves a change in the position or orientation of chromosome segments without net loss or gain of material; the carrier is usually phenotypically normal. An unbalanced rearrangement has extra or missing material (partial trisomy or monosomy) and usually causes malformation and developmental problems.

blocks.markdown: **Deletions and duplications.** A **deletion** is loss of a chromosome segment; it can be *terminal* (loss of the end of an arm) or *interstitial* (loss within an arm). A **duplication** is the gain of an extra copy of a segment. These are unbalanced by definition. Examples of deletion syndromes: **cri-du-chat syndrome** (deletion of part of the short arm of chromosome 5, 5p), with a high-pitched cat-like cry in infancy, microcephaly, hypotonia and intellectual disability; and **22q11.2 deletion syndrome** (DiGeorge syndrome), with outflow-tract cardiac defects, thymic hypoplasia (immune deficiency), hypocalcaemia from parathyroid hypoplasia, cleft palate and facial dysmorphism. Smaller deletions that are too small to see on a standard karyotype are detected by **FISH** or **chromosomal microarray**.

**Translocations.** A **translocation** is the transfer of a segment of one chromosome to another. In a **reciprocal translocation** two non-homologous chromosomes exchange segments; the carrier has 46 chromosomes and, if no material is lost at the breakpoints, is balanced. In a **Robertsonian translocation** the long arms of two **acrocentric** chromosomes (13, 14, 15, 21 and 22, which have very short p arms) fuse at the centromere and the short arms, which carry only repeated ribosomal RNA genes shared with other acrocentrics, are lost. The carrier has **45 chromosomes** but is balanced and healthy because the lost short arms carry no unique genes.

rows: Deletion; duplication; unbalanced translocation product (e.g. translocation Down syndrome)
Unbalanced gametes: infertility, recurrent miscarriage, affected offspring
Often occurs de novo or from a parent carrying a balanced form
blocks.caption: Balanced versus unbalanced chromosomal rearrangements.

blocks.markdown: **Familial Down syndrome and Robertsonian translocation.** Most Down syndrome is a free trisomy 21 due to non-disjunction. About 4% is due to a **Robertsonian translocation** between chromosome 21 and another acrocentric chromosome (most commonly 14). A parent carrying a balanced rob(14;21) has 45 chromosomes: one normal 14, one normal 21 and a fused chromosome containing the long arms of 14 and 21. At meiosis the three chromosomes segregate to produce **six types of gamete**, which on fertilisation by a normal gamete give: normal; balanced carrier; **trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)** because the gamete carries the fusion chromosome plus a free 21; and three non-viable outcomes (monosomy 21, trisomy 14 and monosomy 14), which end as early miscarriage. Hence carriers have a high rate of miscarriage and a risk of a child with Down syndrome that is higher than the age-related risk and is *independent of maternal age*. Empirical recurrence risks are about 10-15% when the mother is the carrier and lower (about 1-3%) when the father is the carrier. The risk is essentially 100% for a carrier of a rob(21;21), because every viable conception is trisomic or monosomic for 21.

blocks.title: Enumerating gametes of a Robertsonian carrier
blocks.prompt: A woman carries a balanced rob(14;21) and her partner has a normal karyotype. List the six possible types of egg and the outcome of fertilisation by a normal sperm in each case.

steps.text: Her three relevant chromosomes are: a normal 14, a normal 21 and the fusion chromosome der(14;21). Meiosis distributes them so that the egg gets one or two of them:
Egg with 14 + 21 gives a normal zygote (46). Egg with the fusion chromosome alone gives a balanced carrier (45).
Egg with the fusion chromosome + 21 provides 14q once and 21q twice. With the sperm's 21 this gives three copies of 21 (translocation trisomy 21, Down syndrome).

Egg with the fusion chromosome + 14 gives three copies of 14, egg with 14 alone gives monosomy 21, and egg with 21 alone gives monosomy 14. All three of these are generally non-viable and end in miscarriage.

Of six equally likely outcomes, 3 are viable (normal, carrier, Down syndrome) and 3 non-viable. In practice the observed risk of a live-born with Down syndrome is lower than the theoretical 1 in 3 among viable fetuses.

blocks.answer: Normal, balanced carrier and translocation Down syndrome are viable; three other combinations are lost, explaining recurrent miscarriage.

blocks.markdown: **Karyotyping.** A **karyotype** is the ordered display of the chromosomes of a cell, usually obtained from dividing cells (cultured lymphocytes, amniocytes, chorionic villi) arrested in metaphase and stained to give a banding pattern, most commonly **G-banding** with Giemsa. Chromosomes are arranged in pairs by size and centromere position; each has a short arm **p** (petit) and a long arm **q**. G-banded karyotyping detects changes in number and larger structural changes (roughly 5-10 million base pairs); smaller changes need **FISH** (fluorescent in situ hybridisation with a labelled probe) or **chromosomal microarray**, and balanced rearrangements are not detected by microarray since there is no change in copy number.

rows: Total number first, then the sex chromosomes
46,XX normal female; 47,XY,+21 male with trisomy 21; 45,X Turner syndrome
Gain or loss of a whole chromosome
5p is the short arm of chromosome 5
46,XX,del(5)(p15): deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 from band p15 (cri-du-chat)
Translocation; chromosomes and breakpoints listed in brackets
46,XY,t(9;22)(q34;q11): reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (the Philadelphia chromosome seen in chronic myeloid leukaemia, an acquired somatic change)
46,XX/47,XX,+21: two cell lines in one person
blocks.caption: Basic ISCN karyotype nomenclature.

blocks.title: Reading a karyotype description

steps.text: (a) A male (XY) with 46 chromosomes and an interstitial/terminal deletion at band q11.2 on the long arm of chromosome 22: an unbalanced rearrangement, the 22q11.2 deletion associated with DiGeorge syndrome.

(b) A female with 46 chromosomes including a Robertsonian derivative chromosome (14;21) plus an additional normal chromosome 21: three copies of 21q in total, so this is translocation (familial) Down syndrome; it is unbalanced.
(c) A male with 45 chromosomes where one derivative chromosome replaces chromosomes 13 and 14: a balanced Robertsonian translocation carrier, phenotypically normal but at risk of unbalanced gametes.

blocks.answer: (a) 22q11.2 deletion, unbalanced; (b) translocation Down syndrome, unbalanced; (c) balanced Robertsonian carrier.

blocks.title: Why karyotype the parents
blocks.text: When a child has translocation Down syndrome, both parents should be karyotyped. If a parent is a balanced carrier, other relatives are at risk and the recurrence risk is much higher than the 1% or less for a free trisomy. If the translocation arose de novo, the recurrence risk is low.

items: Balanced = no net gain or loss, usually healthy carrier; unbalanced = extra or missing material, causes disease.
Robertsonian carrier: 45 chromosomes, fused acrocentric long arms, lost p arms; risk of Down syndrome and miscarriage.
Deletions: cri-du-chat 5p-, 22q11.2 deletion; detected by karyotype if large, FISH or microarray if small.
Karyotype notation: number, sex chromosomes, then abnormalities (del, t, der, +, -, /).

points: Balanced rearrangements (reciprocal or Robertsonian translocations) usually do not harm the carrier, whereas unbalanced ones (deletions, duplications, unbalanced translocations) cause disease.

A carrier of a Robertsonian translocation has 45 chromosomes and may have a child with translocation Down syndrome, with a recurrence risk that depends on the sex of the carrier and not on maternal age.
Karyotype descriptions list the total number, the sex chromosomes and then the abnormality, using symbols such as del, t, der, +, - and the slash for mosaicism.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes a balanced from an unbalanced chromosomal rearrangement?

options.text: A balanced rearrangement has no net loss or gain of genetic material, whereas an unbalanced one does
A balanced rearrangement always causes severe disease, whereas an unbalanced one is harmless
A balanced rearrangement is always acquired, whereas an unbalanced one is always inherited
A balanced rearrangement involves a whole extra chromosome

questions.correctOptionText: A balanced rearrangement has no net loss or gain of genetic material, whereas an unbalanced one does

distractorRationale.b: This is reversed: balanced carriers are usually normal.
distractorRationale.c: Either can be inherited or de novo.
distractorRationale.d: An extra whole chromosome is aneuploidy, not a balanced rearrangement.

questions.explanation: Balanced rearrangements change the arrangement of genetic material without altering its amount, so carriers are usually healthy. Unbalanced ones have extra or missing material and usually cause disease.

questions.stem: A healthy man carries a balanced reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 4 and 11. His partner has had two first-trimester miscarriages. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Some of his gametes carry unbalanced combinations of the translocated chromosomes, producing non-viable embryos
His translocation causes lack of sperm production in every case
The translocation makes his partner's oocytes aneuploid
A balanced translocation makes all of his gametes normal

questions.correctOptionText: Some of his gametes carry unbalanced combinations of the translocated chromosomes, producing non-viable embryos

distractorRationale.a: Correct: segregation at meiosis creates unbalanced gametes with partial trisomy or monosomy.
distractorRationale.b: Many balanced carriers are fertile; the problem is unbalanced gametes.
distractorRationale.c: His chromosomes cannot alter his partner's oocytes.
distractorRationale.d: Meiotic segregation of the rearranged chromosomes generates many unbalanced gametes.

questions.explanation: Although the carrier is healthy, pairing and segregation of the rearranged chromosomes at meiosis produces gametes with partial gains and losses. Embryos from these gametes often miscarry or are malformed.

questions.stem: A mother has the karyotype 45,XX,der(13;14)(q10;q10) and is healthy. Which is the most accurate interpretation?

options.text: A balanced Robertsonian translocation carrier with 45 chromosomes
Turner syndrome
Trisomy 13 in all cells
An unbalanced deletion of chromosome 13

questions.correctOptionText: A balanced Robertsonian translocation carrier with 45 chromosomes

distractorRationale.a: Correct: der(13;14)(q10;q10) is a fusion at the centromeres of two acrocentric chromosomes with no net loss of important material.
distractorRationale.b: Turner syndrome is 45,X, a missing sex chromosome.
distractorRationale.d: A deletion would be indicated by del, with breakpoints.

questions.explanation: The notation shows 45 chromosomes with a derivative chromosome formed from the long arms of 13 and 14 joined at their centromeres (q10;q10). This is a Robertsonian translocation, balanced in this healthy carrier.

questions.stem: A newborn has a high-pitched, cat-like cry, microcephaly, hypotonia and a round face. Which karyotype description best matches the suspected chromosomal abnormality?

options.text: 47,XXY

distractorRationale.a: Correct: deletion of part of the short arm of chromosome 5 causes cri-du-chat syndrome.

questions.explanation: The cat-like cry with microcephaly and hypotonia is cri-du-chat syndrome, caused by a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, written del(5)(p15). The other notations denote numerical abnormalities with different phenotypes.

questions.stem: A cytogenetics report reads 46,XX/47,XX,+21. What does the slash indicate?

options.text: Mosaicism: two cell lines in the same individual
A translocation between chromosomes 46 and 47
That the sample was obtained from two different individuals
A Robertsonian translocation

questions.correctOptionText: Mosaicism: two cell lines in the same individual

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the slash separates different cell lines.
distractorRationale.b: Translocations are indicated by t and bracketed chromosome numbers.
distractorRationale.c: The slash does not imply two individuals.
distractorRationale.d: A Robertsonian translocation would be shown by der or rob in the notation.

questions.explanation: In ISCN nomenclature a slash separates cell lines present in the same individual. This person has a normal female cell line and a cell line with trisomy 21 (mosaic Down syndrome).

questions.stem: A woman carries a balanced rob(14;21) and her partner is chromosomally normal. Assume the six possible gamete types (normal, balanced carrier, trisomy 21, monosomy 21, trisomy 14, monosomy 14 after fertilisation) occur with equal probability and that monosomy 21, trisomy 14 and monosomy 14 conceptions are non-viable. If she conceives 18 times, how many conceptions are expected to be non-viable? Give a number of conceptions.
questions.explanation: Three of the six equally likely zygote types (monosomy 21, trisomy 14, monosomy 14) are non-viable, which is a fraction of 1/2. Of 18 conceptions, 18 x 1/2 = 9 are expected to be non-viable. This model explains the high miscarriage rate in carriers, though actual figures differ.

questions.stem: True or false: A person with a balanced Robertsonian translocation usually has a normal phenotype despite having 45 chromosomes.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The short arms lost in a Robertsonian translocation carry only repeated ribosomal RNA genes shared across acrocentric chromosomes, so no essential genetic material is lost and the carrier is healthy. The risk lies with the carrier's offspring.

questions.stem: A boy has Down syndrome and his karyotype is 46,XY,der(14;21)(q10;q10),+21. His mother is healthy. Explain the likely karyotype of the mother, how the boy's karyotype arose, and why the recurrence risk differs from that of a child with free trisomy 21.
markingGuide: Mother may be a balanced Robertsonian translocation carrier, 45,XX,der(14;21)(q10;q10), with a normal phenotype.
At meiosis the translocation chromosome and a normal 21 can segregate into the same egg; fertilisation by a normal sperm gives three copies of 21q (the boy's karyotype).
The boy's cells have 46 chromosomes but trisomy for the long arm of 21 (unbalanced).

Recurrence risk for a carrier is much higher (empirically about 10-15% for a carrier mother, lower for a carrier father) and not related to maternal age, whereas free trisomy has a low recurrence risk (about 1% or less) and is age-related.
Carriers also have increased miscarriage from other unbalanced gametes; parental karyotyping and counselling are required.
questions.explanation: A parental balanced Robertsonian translocation allows unbalanced gametes carrying the fusion chromosome and an extra 21. This translocation Down syndrome is familial and recurrence risk depends on carrier status and sex.

questions.stem: Interpret each of the following karyotypes: (a) 47,XY,+18; (b) 46,XX,t(2;7)(p21;q36); (c) 46,XY,del(22)(q11.2). State whether each is balanced or unbalanced and name a likely consequence.
markingGuide: (a) Male with an extra chromosome 18 (trisomy 18, Edwards syndrome); numerical and unbalanced; severe malformations.

(b) Female with a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 2 and 7, breakpoints 2p21 and 7q36; if no material is lost it is balanced, with a normal carrier phenotype but risk of unbalanced gametes and miscarriage.
(c) Male with a deletion at 22q11.2: unbalanced, DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome with cardiac, thymic, parathyroid and palatal anomalies.
Correct use of the order of number, sex chromosomes and abnormality.
questions.explanation: Reading a karyotype means taking the chromosome number, the sex chromosomes and then each abnormality with its breakpoints. Net gain or loss decides whether it is unbalanced.

questions.stem: A phenotypically normal woman with a balanced Robertsonian translocation rob(21;21) is expecting a baby with a normal partner. Which statement about the pregnancy is correct?

options.text: Every viable conception is expected to have Down syndrome
Half of conceptions will be normal and half will be balanced carriers
The risk of Down syndrome is the same as the maternal age-related risk
All conceptions will be normal because the translocation is balanced

questions.correctOptionText: Every viable conception is expected to have Down syndrome

distractorRationale.a: Correct: her gametes carry either both chromosome 21 long arms (giving trisomy 21) or none (monosomy 21, non-viable).
distractorRationale.b: Normal or balanced-carrier offspring would require a gamete with one copy of 21, which this carrier cannot produce since both copies are fused.
distractorRationale.c: Her risk is far above age-related risk and independent of age.
distractorRationale.d: A balanced carrier is healthy but her gametes are unbalanced.

questions.explanation: A carrier of rob(21;21) has both chromosome 21 copies fused into one chromosome, so each gamete contains either two copies of 21q or none. Fertilisation gives trisomy 21 (live-born Down syndrome) or monosomy 21 (non-viable), so every viable conception is affected.
